why: The product backlog is where a Product Owner’s decisions become visible: what the team builds next, what waits and what never gets built. Hiring managers test it directly, with a backlog to order, an epic to split or a stakeholder who wants their feature first, because a PO who cannot slice, prioritise and say no wastes a whole team’s Sprints.
outcome: own a product backlog the way the Scrum Guide describes it, split epics into thin vertical stories, write acceptance criteria and a Definition of Done that hold, run refinement with the Developers, compare items with cost of delay, WSJF, RICE and ICE in a spreadsheet, use MoSCoW and Kano where they fit, and keep the backlog small, honest and visible.

lessons.title: The product backlog in Scrum
text: The Scrum Guide 2020 defines the Product Backlog as an emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, and the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team. Emergent means it is never finished: it changes as the team learns from users, the market and each Increment. Single source means there is no side list in a manager’s inbox: if work is not in the backlog, the team should not be doing it.

Each Scrum artifact has a commitment, and the backlog’s commitment is the Product Goal: the future state of the product the team is working towards, for example “small shops can run their whole returns process in our app by the end of the year”. The Scrum Team should fulfil (or abandon) one Product Goal before taking on the next. Every item in the backlog should help reach it; an item you cannot connect to the goal is a candidate for removal or a sign that the goal is unclear.

The Product Owner is accountable for maximising the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and for effective Product Backlog management: developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal, creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items, ordering them, and ensuring the backlog is transparent, visible and understood. The PO may delegate some of this work, for example letting a Developer write a technical item, but remains accountable. The PO is one person, not a committee, and people who want to change the backlog do it by convincing the PO.

The Scrum Guide says ordered, not prioritised, and the difference matters. Priority labels (“High” on 140 tickets) let everything be important; an order forces one sequence with no ties, so the question becomes “this before that?”. The order weighs value, cost of delay, risk, dependencies and what the team needs to learn. A healthy backlog looks like an iceberg, often summarised as DEEP (Roman Pichler and Mike Cohn): Detailed appropriately, Estimated, Emergent, Prioritised. Items near the top are small, clear and sized; items further down stay coarse until they get closer.

Do not confuse the Product Backlog with the Sprint Backlog. The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers: the Sprint Goal (why), the items selected for the Sprint (what) and their plan to deliver them (how). The PO orders the Product Backlog and agrees the Sprint Goal with the team at Sprint Planning, but does not assign tasks or add work to the Sprint behind the Developers’ backs. Interviewers often ask “what exactly does the PO own?”; the answer above, in the Scrum Guide’s own words, scores well.
points: Product Backlog: emergent, ordered, the single source of work for the Scrum Team.
Its commitment is the Product Goal; every item should serve it.
The PO is accountable for backlog management, even when someone else writes items.
Ordered, not prioritised: one sequence, no ties.
The Sprint Backlog belongs to the Developers; the PO does not assign tasks.

example.code:
PRODUCT GOAL: small shops run their whole returns process in our app by December

#  Item                                         Size  State
1  Customer starts a return from the order page   5    Ready (AC + sized)
2  Shop approves or refuses a return              3    Ready
3  Prepaid return label (one carrier)             8    Ready
4  Refund to the original card                    5    Being refined
5  Return reasons report for the shop            ~13   Needs splitting
6  Exchanges instead of refunds                  L     Idea (epic)
7  Second and third carriers                     L     Idea (epic)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Top: small, detailed, sized.  Bottom: coarse, cheap to change.
example.note: One goal, one order, detail that grows as items rise: the iceberg in practice.

lessons.title: Epics, features, stories and slicing
text: The Scrum Guide only speaks of Product Backlog items; epics, features and stories are conventions from tools and frameworks. In Jira an epic groups stories; SAFe uses epic → capability → feature → story. Use the vocabulary of the organisation, but keep the idea: big items are fine at the bottom of the backlog, and they are split into stories small enough to finish within one Sprint before the team selects them. The basics of the story format (“As a…, I want…, so that…”) and Given/When/Then are in the Requirements & user stories course; this lesson is about splitting well.

Split vertically, not horizontally. A vertical slice goes through every layer the feature needs (screen, API, database, tests) and gives a user something they can use and the team something it can demo and measure. A horizontal slice (“build the database tables”, “do the API”, “do the UI”) delivers nothing on its own and hides risk until the last piece is joined. A thin vertical slice with an ugly screen beats three finished layers that do not work together.

INVEST, from Bill Wake (2003), is the classic check for a good story: Independent (can be built and released in any order, as far as possible), Negotiable (the details are a conversation, not a contract), Valuable (to a user or customer), Estimable (the team understands it enough to size it), Small (fits comfortably in a Sprint, ideally a few days), Testable (you can say when it is done). Ron Jeffries’ three Cs remind you that the card is only a placeholder: Card, Conversation, Confirmation.

Splitting patterns give you ready-made cuts. Workflow steps: one story per step of the journey, or the simplest end-to-end path first. Business rule variations: one rule per story (standard shipping first, express later). Happy path first, then the error and exception paths. Data variations: one country, one currency or one file format first. Interfaces: web first, mobile app later. Operations: create and view before edit and delete. Defer performance: make it work, then make it fast. When the team simply does not know enough, a timeboxed spike answers the question first. Mike Cohn’s SPIDR groups the same ideas: Spike, Paths, Interfaces, Data, Rules.

In real backlogs the common failures are stories split by team or component (“front-end story”, “back-end story”), stories that are tasks in disguise, and epics that never get split because nobody owns the conversation. A good test: after splitting, can you release the first story alone and learn something? If the answer is no, cut again. Interviewers love “split this epic for me”: name the user, the outcome, the first thin end-to-end slice, and what you deliberately leave for later.
points: Vertical slices cross every layer and can be demoed; horizontal slices cannot.
INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Card, Conversation, Confirmation: the card is a reminder of a conversation.
Split by workflow step, rule, happy path, data, interface or operation; spike the unknowns.
After a split, the first story should be releasable on its own.

example.code:
EPIC: Online returns for a shoe shop

Horizontal (avoid)            Vertical slices (prefer)
- Returns database tables     1. Customer requests a return for one item,
- Returns API                     shop gets an e-mail          (happy path)
- Returns screens             2. Shop approves or refuses in the back office
- Carrier integration         3. Customer downloads a prepaid label, one carrier
                              4. Refund to the original card after approval
                              5. Return of several items in one request  (data)
                              6. Returns outside the 30-day window refused (rule)
                              7. Same flow in the mobile app        (interface)
example.note: Slice 1 is ugly but real: a customer can return a pair of shoes and the shop learns how often it happens.

lessons.title: Acceptance criteria, definition of ready and definition of done
text: Acceptance criteria are the conditions one specific item must meet to be accepted: they belong to the story. Write them as a short rule list (“refund goes to the original card”, “a return after 30 days is refused with a message”) or as Given/When/Then scenarios when behaviour depends on context (see the Requirements & user stories course). Good criteria are testable, cover at least one negative path, describe behaviour rather than implementation, and are agreed with the Developers and testers in refinement, not handed over at Sprint Planning.

The Definition of Done is different: it is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product (Scrum Guide 2020). It applies to every item, it is the commitment of the Increment, and it typically lists things like code reviewed, automated tests passing, deployed to the staging environment, accessibility checked, documentation updated. If the organisation has a Definition of Done as a standard, every Scrum Team follows it as a minimum; otherwise the Scrum Team creates one for the product.

The consequence is strict: if an item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog for future consideration. “Done except testing” is not done. This protects transparency: stakeholders see only work that is truly usable, and the team does not pile up hidden work for later. A PO who accepts half-done work to make the review look good creates technical debt and false forecasts.

The Definition of Ready is not in the Scrum Guide. Many teams use one as a working agreement for what an item needs before Sprint Planning: a clear user and outcome, acceptance criteria, sized by the Developers, small enough for one Sprint, dependencies known. The Scrum Guide only says that items which can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection. Keep a DoR light: when it becomes a long gate with sign-offs, it turns refinement into a mini waterfall and stops useful conversations from happening during the Sprint.

In interviews, the classic trap is “what is the difference between acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done?”. Answer: acceptance criteria are specific to one item and say what it must do; the Definition of Done is shared by all items and says what quality level everything must reach. An item is complete when both are met.
points: Acceptance criteria: per item, testable, include a negative path.
Definition of Done: for every item, the quality bar of the Increment.
Not Done means not released and not shown at the Sprint Review: back to the backlog.
Definition of Ready: a team convention, not Scrum; keep it short.
Complete = acceptance criteria met AND Definition of Done met.

example.code:
STORY: Refund to the original card after approval
Acceptance criteria (this story only)
  - Refund is sent within 1 hour of the shop's approval
  - Amount = item price; shipping is refunded only if the whole order is returned
  - If the card has expired, the shop sees "refund failed" and a manual option
  - Customer gets an e-mail with the amount and the expected delay

DEFINITION OF DONE (every item)
  [ ] Code reviewed by another Developer
  [ ] Unit and API tests pass in the pipeline
  [ ] Deployed to staging and checked against the acceptance criteria
  [ ] No new critical accessibility issue
  [ ] Monitoring and help text updated
example.note: The top block changes with every story; the bottom block is the same for all of them.

lessons.title: Refinement and estimation
text: Product Backlog refinement is, in the Scrum Guide’s words, the act of breaking down and further defining items into smaller, more precise items: an ongoing activity that adds details such as a description, order and size. It is not one of the five Scrum events, so teams organise it as they like, often one or two sessions a week. Older versions of the Scrum Guide said it usually takes no more than 10 % of the Developers’ capacity; the 2020 version gives no number. The PO brings the why and the context, the Developers bring the how and the risks, and the best sessions end with fewer questions and smaller items.

The Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing. The PO can help them understand an item and select trade-offs (“what if we drop the PDF and send an e-mail?”), but does not estimate for them, and neither does a manager. Estimates are the team’s forecast, not a promise, and they include everything needed to meet the Definition of Done.

Story points are a relative measure of size: effort, complexity and uncertainty together, compared with a reference story the whole team knows (“the password reset was a 3”). Teams use a modified Fibonacci scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20, 40, 100) because the gaps grow with size: nobody can tell a 14 from a 15. In Planning Poker each Developer picks a card in secret, everyone reveals at once, the highest and lowest explain their reasons, and the team votes again. The discussion is the real value: a 2 and a 13 on the same story mean someone knows something the others do not. For epics, T-shirt sizes (S, M, L, XL) are enough.

Velocity is the number of points of Done work per Sprint. Use it as a range for forecasting, not as a target: if the last three Sprints delivered 34, 28 and 31 points, plan around 31 and say “28 to 34”. Points are not comparable between teams, and turning velocity into a performance goal makes points inflate (Goodhart’s law: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring). Some teams skip points and count items, which works once stories are split to similar sizes.

What goes wrong in real jobs: refining items that will not be built for months, estimating in hours and then being judged on them, the PO arguing a number down, and Sprint Planning turned into refinement because nothing was ready. A simple rule helps: keep roughly the next two Sprints of items refined and sized, and refine further only what is likely to be built.
points: Refinement: ongoing, adds description, order and size; not a Scrum event.
The Developers size the work; the PO explains and offers trade-offs.
Story points are relative, on a modified Fibonacci scale, against a reference story.
Planning Poker: secret vote, reveal, the extremes explain, vote again.
Velocity forecasts as a range; it is never a target or a team comparison.

example.code:
A          B             C   D                        E
1    Sprint     Points done       Planned item             Points
2    Sprint 21  34                Login with SSO           8
3    Sprint 22  28                Saved searches           5
4    Sprint 23  31                Bulk import, CSV only    13
5                                 Fix export timeout       3

Forecast  =AVERAGE(B2:B4)              -> 31
Range     =MIN(B2:B4)  to  =MAX(B2:B4) -> 28 to 34
Planned   =SUM(E2:E5)                  -> 29
Room left =AVERAGE(B2:B4)-SUM(E2:E5)   -> 2
example.note: With 2 points of room, a 3-point story does not fit on average; say so before the Sprint, not after.

lessons.title: Value vs effort and cost of delay
text: The simplest prioritisation tool is a value / effort matrix: place each item on two axes and you get four boxes. Quick wins (high value, low effort) go first; big bets (high value, high effort) are planned and sliced; fill-ins (low value, low effort) wait for spare capacity; money pits (low value, high effort) are usually dropped. It is rough and relative, which is exactly why it works in a 30-minute workshop with stakeholders, and why it should not be the only tool for a large backlog.

Value needs a definition before it can be compared. It can be revenue, cost saved, risk reduced (security, compliance, a fragile system), learning (an experiment that tells you whether a bigger bet is worth it) or customer satisfaction. Always ask “value for whom, and how will we know?”: an item with a metric you can watch after release is easier to defend than one that is “strategic”.

Cost of delay, popularised by Don Reinertsen (The Principles of Product Development Flow, 2009), asks what it costs per week not to have an item. It turns “urgent” into a number you can compare. When two items compete for the same team, divide cost of delay by duration (CD3) and do the highest first. Example: A costs 10k per week of delay and takes 4 weeks; B costs 6k per week and takes 1 week. A first: B waits 4 weeks, 4 × 6k = 24k lost. B first: A waits 1 week, 10k lost. CD3 says the same: A = 10 / 4 = 2.5, B = 6 / 1 = 6, so B goes first even though A is worth more per week.

WSJF (Weighted Shortest Job First) is SAFe’s version of the same idea. Cost of delay is the sum of three relative scores: user-business value, time criticality, and risk reduction / opportunity enablement. WSJF = cost of delay / job size. Teams score each column on the modified Fibonacci scale, one column at a time across all items, giving the smallest item in each column a 1. A regulatory fix with a hard deadline and a small size can then beat a large, valuable feature, which is usually the right call.

The limits are human, not mathematical. Scores are relative guesses; people learn to inflate the columns that favour their item; job size is sometimes confused with effort in days. Treat the result as an input to a conversation, show the scores openly, and revisit them when something changes (a deadline moves, a competitor launches). Interviewers like to hear that you use these tools to make trade-offs explicit, not to hide behind a number.
points: Value / effort: quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pits; good for a first sort.
Define value: revenue, cost, risk, learning or satisfaction, with a metric.
Cost of delay = what each week without the item costs.
CD3 = cost of delay / duration: short, urgent items first.
WSJF = (user-business value + time criticality + risk reduction / opportunity enablement) / job size.

example.code:
A                      B      C      D       E               F          G
1    Feature                Value  Time   Risk    Cost of delay   Job size   WSJF
2    Consent banner fix     5      13     8       =B2+C2+D2       3          =E2/F2
3    Self-service refunds   13     5      3       =B3+C3+D3       8          =E3/F3
4    Partner API            8      3      13      =B4+C4+D4       13         =E4/F4

Results: consent fix 26/3 = 8.67, refunds 21/8 = 2.63, partner API 24/13 = 1.85
example.note: The small fix with a deadline goes first, even though the refunds feature has the highest business value.

lessons.title: RICE and ICE scoring
text: RICE was published by Intercom to compare product ideas on the same scale. Reach: how many people or events the item affects in a period (customers per quarter, transactions per month). Impact: how much it moves the goal for each person, on a fixed scale: 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal. Confidence: how sure you are of the other numbers: 100 % high, 80 % medium, 50 % low. Effort: person-months of work from everyone involved. RICE score = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort.

A worked example. Bulk import reaches 800 customers a quarter, impact 2, confidence 80 %, effort 2 person-months: 800 × 2 × 0.8 / 2 = 640. Better search filters reach 5,000, impact 0.5, confidence 100 %, effort 1: 2,500. A new onboarding reaches 3,000, impact 1, confidence 50 %, effort 3: 500. The modest feature that many people use wins, which is often the useful surprise of RICE; the onboarding scores low mainly because nobody has evidence yet, so a small experiment to raise confidence may be the real next step.

In a spreadsheet, compute the score in one column (=B2*C2*D2/E2), then find the top item with =INDEX(A2:A4,MATCH(MAX(F2:F4),F2:F4,0)): MAX finds the best score, MATCH finds its row, INDEX returns the name. Keep the inputs visible so anyone can challenge a number, and write down where Reach comes from (analytics, support tickets, sales pipeline).

ICE, associated with Sean Ellis and growth teams, is lighter: Impact, Confidence and Ease, each scored from 1 to 10. Most teams multiply them (8 × 5 × 6 = 240), some average them (6.3); pick one and keep it. Ease is the inverse of effort, so higher is better. ICE fits a stream of small experiments (onboarding e-mails, landing page tests) where speed of decision matters more than precision; RICE fits product features where reach can be measured.

Both have the same weaknesses: one optimistic person scoring alone, impact chosen to get the answer you wanted, and items that must happen anyway (a legal obligation, a security fix) forced through a scoring they do not need. Score together, calibrate against items you have already shipped (“what did we say the impact of saved searches would be, and what happened?”), and treat mandatory work separately.
points: RICE = Reach × Impact × Confidence / Effort.
Impact scale 3 / 2 / 1 / 0.5 / 0.25; confidence 100 / 80 / 50 %; effort in person-months.
Top item in a sheet: INDEX / MATCH of MAX.
ICE = Impact, Confidence, Ease from 1 to 10, for fast experiments.
Low confidence is a signal to learn first, not only to wait.

example.code:
A                B      C       D           E        F
1    Item             Reach  Impact  Confidence  Effort   RICE
2    Bulk import      800    2       0.8         2        =B2*C2*D2/E2   -> 640
3    Search filters   5000   0.5     1           1        =B3*C3*D3/E3   -> 2500
4    New onboarding   3000   1       0.5         3        =B4*C4*D4/E4   -> 500

Top item: =INDEX(A2:A4,MATCH(MAX(F2:F4),F2:F4,0))   -> Search filters
ICE:      =8*5*6 -> 240   (Impact 8, Confidence 5, Ease 6)
example.note: Same formula on every row; the top item follows the scores when an input changes.

lessons.title: MoSCoW, Kano and when each fits
text: MoSCoW was created by Dai Clegg at Oracle in 1994 and became part of DSDM (now the Agile Business Consortium’s method). Must have: without it the release is useless, illegal or unsafe; ask “what happens if it is not there?” and if the answer is “we would release anyway with a workaround”, it is not a Must. Should have: important, painful to leave out, but there is a workaround. Could have: desirable, the first to drop when time runs short. Won’t have this time: agreed out of scope for this release, which is as useful as the Musts because it stops the same debate every week.

DSDM guidance is to keep Must haves to no more than about 60 % of the effort of a timebox, with Could haves around 20 % as contingency. When everything is a Must, MoSCoW is useless: push back with the “what happens if not?” question and with dates. MoSCoW fits a fixed date or fixed budget release where the conversation is about scope with stakeholders; it does not order items within a category, so pair it with a scoring or simple ranking.

The Kano model, from Noriaki Kano (1984), looks at features from the customer’s satisfaction. Must-be (basic) features cause anger when missing and no delight when present: a banking app that shows the right balance. One-dimensional (performance) features satisfy more the better they are: faster transfers, lower fees. Attractive features (delighters) are not expected, so their absence costs nothing but their presence delights: a spending insight nobody asked for. Indifferent features nobody cares about, and reverse features annoy some users (more notifications).

Kano is measured with paired questions to users: “How would you feel if the app had this?” and “How would you feel if it did not?”, each answered with I like it, I expect it, I am neutral, I can tolerate it, I dislike it. The combination classifies the feature. Categories move over time: yesterday’s delighter (contactless payment, live tracking of a delivery) becomes today’s basic expectation, so re-check the classification every year or two.

When each fits: Kano to understand what customers value and avoid over-investing in basics; RICE or WSJF to rank a long list with numbers; cost of delay when timing matters; MoSCoW to negotiate the scope of a fixed release; value / effort for a first sort in a workshop. Mature POs combine them, for example Kano to find the basics that must be solid, then RICE to rank the performance and attractive ideas. The Requirements & user stories course has the basic definitions; here the point is choosing the right tool for the decision in front of you.
points: MoSCoW: Must, Should, Could, Won’t have this time; test a Must with “what happens if not?”.
DSDM: Musts at most about 60 % of the effort, Coulds about 20 % as contingency.
Kano: must-be, one-dimensional (performance), attractive, indifferent, reverse.
Delighters become basic expectations over time.
Pick the tool for the decision: understand (Kano), rank (RICE, WSJF), negotiate scope (MoSCoW).

example.code:
KANO QUESTION PAIR (banking app, feature: instant transfer to a friend)
  If the app HAS it:      I like it / I expect it / neutral / I can tolerate it / I dislike it
  If the app DOES NOT:    I like it / I expect it / neutral / I can tolerate it / I dislike it

  Has = "I like it"   + Does not = "I dislike it"  -> one-dimensional (performance)
  Has = "I like it"   + Does not = "neutral"       -> attractive (delighter)
  Has = "I expect it" + Does not = "I dislike it"  -> must-be (basic)
  Has = "neutral"     + Does not = "neutral"       -> indifferent

MOSCOW (release on 1 March, fixed date)
  Must:   login, balance, transfer to saved payee
  Should: transfer to a new payee with confirmation code
  Could:  spending categories
  Won't (this time): savings goals
example.note: Kano tells you how customers feel about a feature; MoSCoW decides what this release contains.

lessons.title: Keeping the backlog healthy
text: A backlog of 800 items is not transparent: nobody reads it, and the order below the first 50 means nothing. Prune regularly. A common team rule is to archive items nobody has touched for six months, with a note; if they matter, they come back. Keep about two Sprints of items ready at the top, the next few months as features, and everything beyond as a short list of epics or themes linked to the Product Goal. Saying “it is in the backlog” to a stakeholder when the item will never be built is a polite lie.

Technical debt (a metaphor from Ward Cunningham, 1992) and bugs belong in the same backlog, ordered against features, because they compete for the same team. Make debt visible with items that state the business effect (“checkout changes take three times longer because of the old payment module”), not just “refactor X”. Some teams also agree a regular share of capacity for maintenance; either way, the PO decides with the Developers, who know where the risk is. The Definition of Done is the best prevention: work that meets it does not create new hidden debt.

Bugs need a simple rule agreed with the team: a critical production bug (people cannot pay, data is wrong) is fixed now, even mid-Sprint; other bugs become backlog items and are ordered like anything else; a bug found in a story of the current Sprint is simply part of finishing that story. Without the rule, every bug becomes an emergency and the Sprint Goal is lost.

Saying no is part of the job. A good no explains the reason in terms of the Product Goal, offers what is possible (a smaller version, a workaround, a date to review it again) and is recorded so the same request does not come back every week. “Not now, because this quarter we are focused on returns; the export can be done by hand with this report; I will review it in June” keeps the relationship and the focus. A decision log with the date, the request, the decision and the reason is cheap and protects the PO later.

Transparency closes the loop. Keep the backlog readable by stakeholders (clear titles, no internal jargon), show the order and the reasons at the Sprint Review, and tell people when their item moves down, before they find out. A monthly backlog health check takes 30 minutes and avoids most of the problems above.
points: Prune: archive untouched items; keep about two Sprints ready, the rest coarse.
Technical debt and bugs are ordered in the same backlog as features.
State debt in business terms; the Definition of Done prevents new debt.
A good no gives the reason, an alternative and a review date, and is recorded.
Tell stakeholders when their item moves down, before they discover it.

example.code:
MONTHLY BACKLOG HEALTH CHECK (30 min)
[ ] Product Goal still true? Every top-20 item linked to it
[ ] Top 2 Sprints: items ready (AC, sized, fit in a Sprint)
[ ] Items untouched for 6 months: archived with a note
[ ] Duplicates merged; vague titles rewritten
[ ] Technical debt and bugs visible, stated in business terms
[ ] Stakeholders told about items that moved down
[ ] Decision log updated (request, decision, reason, review date)

Backlog size: 412 -> 138 items after pruning
example.note: A short, ordered backlog is easier to explain, to defend and to change.

Commitment of the Product Backlog: the future state of the product
Accountable for maximising value and for backlog management
Sprint Goal + selected items + plan, owned by the Developers
One sequence with no ties, not priority labels
Large item split into stories before selection
Crosses every layer and can be demoed
One layer only (tables, API): no value alone
Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable
Spike, Paths, Interfaces, Data, Rules: ways to split
Timeboxed research to answer an unknown
Conditions one specific item must meet
Quality bar of the Increment, for every item
Team convention before selection; not in the Scrum Guide
Not released, not shown at the Sprint Review, back to the backlog
Ongoing: adds description, order and size
Secret vote, reveal, extremes explain, vote again
Points of Done work per Sprint: a forecast range
The Developers who will do the work
What each week without the item costs
Cost of delay / duration: highest first
(Value + time criticality + risk reduction) / job size
Name of the item with the top score
Must, Should, Could, Won’t have this time
Without it the release is useless, illegal or unsafe
Expected: absence angers, presence does not delight
Quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pits

pitfalls: Labelling half the backlog “High priority” instead of putting it in one order.
Splitting work by layer or by team (front-end story, back-end story) instead of vertical slices.
Accepting “done except testing” at the Sprint Review: it is not Done and hides work.
Estimating for the Developers, or turning velocity into a target to compare teams.
Hiding behind a RICE or WSJF score instead of using it to explain a trade-off.
Marking everything as a Must, so MoSCoW no longer helps decide anything.
Letting the backlog grow to hundreds of items that will never be built.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: in H2, return the name of the item with the highest RICE score (INDEX / MATCH of MAX).
exercises.hint: MAX(F2:F6) finds the best score, MATCH(…,F2:F6,0) finds its position, INDEX(A2:A6,…) returns the name.
exercises.explain: =INDEX(A2:A6,MATCH(MAX(F2:F6),F2:F6,0)) returns Saved searches (3200). The 0 in MATCH asks for an exact match; the result changes by itself when the scores change.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: in F2, compute the WSJF of “Payment retry” (cost of delay = business value + time criticality + risk reduction, divided by job size).
exercises.hint: Add the three cost of delay columns first (brackets), then divide by the job size.
exercises.explain: =(B2+C2+D2)/E2 gives (8 + 13 + 5) / 8 = 3.25. Without the brackets Excel would divide only D2 by E2. Invoice PDF scores 10 / 3 = 3.33 and Partner API 23 / 13 = 1.77, so the small invoice item edges ahead.

exercises.q: Excel on a real sheet: in G2, how many points of room are left in the next Sprint if the forecast is the average velocity of the last three Sprints and the items in E2:E5 are already planned?
exercises.hint: Forecast = AVERAGE of the three velocities; subtract the SUM of the planned points.
exercises.explain: =AVERAGE(B2:B4)-SUM(E2:E5) gives 31 − 29 = 2 points. A 3-point story does not fit on average; the Developers decide at Sprint Planning, and the PO knows in advance which trade-off to propose.

exercises.q: A big item arrives: “Customers can pay in instalments”. Put the refinement steps in order.
steps: Restate the problem, the user and the link to the Product Goal
Map the steps the customer goes through
Slice into thin vertical stories, simplest end-to-end path first
Write acceptance criteria for the top slices
Developers size the slices and split again anything too big for a Sprint
Re-order the backlog with the new slices
exercises.answer: Why and for whom first, then the journey, then vertical slices, then criteria for the slices that are close, then sizing by the Developers (which may trigger another split), and finally the order. Sizing before slicing would estimate an epic; ordering before sizing ignores effort.

exercises.q: Sort these backlog items: which are good user stories, and which need rework before refinement?

groups.name: Good story
items: As a returning customer, I want to reorder a past order in one tap so that my weekly shop is faster
As a support agent, I want to see a customer’s last five orders on the ticket so that I can answer without switching tools
As a shop owner, I want to export this month’s sales as CSV so that my accountant can import them

groups.name: Needs rework
items: Create the orders table in the database
As a user, I want the app to be better

exercises.answer: The good stories name a user, an action and a benefit, are small and testable. The orders table is a horizontal slice with no value alone; “better” cannot be tested or estimated; the loyalty programme is an epic that must be split.

exercises.q: Food delivery app: sort these features into Kano categories, as most customers today would see them.

groups.name: Must-be (basic)
items: The order matches what was ordered
The total price is shown before paying

groups.name: One-dimensional (performance)
items: Number of restaurants to choose from

groups.name: Attractive (delighter)
items: A surprise free dessert on your birthday
Dish suggestions that match your past orders

exercises.answer: Basics only cause anger when missing; performance features satisfy more the better they are; delighters please because nobody expects them. Categories move: live tracking of the courier was a delighter and is now expected, so a real Kano survey is worth repeating.

exercises.q: Match each technique with the situation it fits best.
pairs: Ranking many feature ideas when you can measure how many users each affects
Sequencing large features when deadlines and risk matter
Agreeing the scope of a fixed-date release with stakeholders
Finding which features customers expect and which would delight them
Quickly ranking a stream of small growth experiments
A first rough sort of ideas in a short workshop
exercises.answer: Each tool answers a different question; mature POs combine them, for example Kano to understand, RICE or WSJF to rank, MoSCoW to negotiate the release scope.

exercises.q: Sprint Review. The sales director says: “Our biggest client renews next month only if they get bulk import. Promise me it for the end of the next Sprint.” What do you do?

steps.text: Your first answer in the meeting?

choices.label: Thank them, ask what the client really needs to do and what is at stake, and say you will assess it with the team before Sprint Planning
choices.feedback: You take the request seriously and learn the real problem (maybe a one-off CSV of 2,000 products) without promising what the Developers have not forecast.

choices.label: Promise it: the client is too important to refuse
choices.feedback: Only the Developers can forecast what fits in a Sprint. A public promise you may not keep hurts the team and the client.

choices.label: Refuse: the backlog order is already decided
choices.feedback: The backlog is emergent. A renewal at risk is new information worth weighing; a flat no damages the relationship.

steps.text: The renewal is worth far more per week of delay than the current top item. The full feature is about 40 points. What next?

choices.label: Slice it: a first story covering the client’s CSV template only, refined with the Developers and moved to the top
choices.feedback: Cost of delay justifies moving it up, and a thin slice can realistically be Done in one Sprint.

choices.label: Put the full 40-point feature at the top of the next Sprint
choices.feedback: Far above the team’s velocity: the Sprint Goal would fail and nothing would be Done.

choices.label: Cancel the current Sprint to start now
choices.feedback: A Sprint is cancelled only when its Sprint Goal becomes obsolete; this request can wait for the next Sprint Planning.

steps.text: At Sprint Planning the Developers say the slice fits only if the “saved searches” story waits one Sprint. Then?

choices.label: Accept the trade-off, update the backlog and tell the stakeholders of saved searches why it moved, before they find out
choices.feedback: The order is the PO’s decision, made in the open; people whose item moved down hear it from you with the reason.

choices.label: Ask the Developers to squeeze both in
choices.feedback: Overloading the Sprint trades a clear decision for overtime and a likely miss on both.

exercises.answer: Listen and find the real need, weigh it with cost of delay, slice it to what can be Done in one Sprint, let the Developers forecast, and make the trade-off visible to everyone affected.

exercises.q: An idea reaches 2,000 customers per quarter, impact 1 (medium), confidence 50 %, effort 4 person-months. What is its RICE score?
exercises.answer: 2,000 × 1 × 0.5 / 4 = 250. Low confidence halves the score: a quick test to raise confidence may be worth more than building it.

exercises.q: At the end of the Sprint, a story works on the test environment and meets its acceptance criteria, but the performance tests required by the Definition of Done were not run. According to the Scrum Guide 2020, what happens?
options: Show it as done at the Sprint Review and run the tests next Sprint
It is not part of the Increment: it is not presented as done and returns to the Product Backlog
The Product Owner can accept it because the acceptance criteria are met
The Sprint is extended by two days to finish the tests
exercises.answer: An item that does not meet the Definition of Done cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review; it returns to the Product Backlog. Acceptance criteria alone are not enough, and Sprints have a fixed length.

exercises.q: Split the epic “Customers can manage their subscription online” (today they must call support) into 5 to 7 vertical stories, in order, and say which one you would release first and why.
exercises.answer: 1) As a subscriber, I want to see my current plan, price and next billing date, so that I stop calling support to ask (read-only, smallest, removes many calls). 2) As a subscriber, I want to update my card, so that my subscription does not stop when my card expires (failed payments cost revenue). 3) As a subscriber, I want to switch to a higher plan, effective now with a prorated charge (revenue, happy path). 4) As a subscriber, I want to switch to a lower plan from the next billing date (business rule variation). 5) As a subscriber, I want to pause for up to two months instead of cancelling (retention). 6) As a subscriber, I want to cancel online and get a confirmation e-mail (legal and trust; in many countries online cancellation must be easy). 7) Same flows in the mobile app (interface). First release: story 1, because it is thin, crosses every layer, can ship in days and reduces support calls you can measure; story 2 follows because failed payments have a clear cost of delay. Each story gets acceptance criteria, for example the price shown matches the invoice and a cancelled plan stays active until the end of the paid period.

interview.q: What is the Product Owner accountable for?
interview.a: In the Scrum Guide 2020, for maximising the value of the product resulting from the Scrum Team’s work, and for effective Product Backlog management: developing and communicating the Product Goal, creating and clearly communicating backlog items, ordering them, and keeping the backlog transparent, visible and understood. I can delegate writing items, but the accountability stays with me, and I do not manage the Developers’ tasks.

interview.q: How do you split a large epic?
interview.a: I start from the user and the outcome, map the journey, and look for the thinnest end-to-end slice that a user can use and we can measure. Then I split by workflow step, business rule, happy path then exceptions, data variation or interface, and use a timeboxed spike where we do not know enough. I check each story with INVEST and avoid layer-by-layer stories, because they deliver nothing until the last one is done.

interview.q: What is the difference between acceptance criteria and the Definition of Done?
interview.a: Acceptance criteria belong to one item and say what it must do, including the negative paths. The Definition of Done applies to every item and describes the quality of the Increment: reviewed, tested, deployed to staging, documented. An item is complete only when both are met; if it misses the DoD it is not shown at the Sprint Review and goes back to the backlog.

interview.q: How do you prioritise the backlog?
interview.a: I order it against the Product Goal. For a long list of features I use RICE or WSJF to compare value, urgency and size, cost of delay when timing matters, Kano to understand what customers expect, and MoSCoW when we negotiate the scope of a fixed-date release. The scores are inputs: I share them openly, check them with data, and treat mandatory items such as a legal fix separately.

interview.q: A stakeholder insists their feature must go first. What do you do?
interview.a: I listen for the real problem and the cost of waiting, compare it with what is above it using the same criteria as everything else, and look for a smaller slice that answers the urgent part. Then I decide, explain the reason in terms of the Product Goal, and if the answer is not now, offer a workaround and a review date and record the decision. The people whose items move down hear it from me.

interview.q: Do you estimate the stories? How do you use velocity?
interview.a: No, the Developers who will do the work size it, usually in story points with Planning Poker; I explain the need and offer trade-offs to reduce the size. I use velocity as a range for forecasting, for example 28 to 34 points, never as a target or to compare teams, because then the points inflate and stop meaning anything.

interview.q: How do you handle technical debt and bugs?
interview.a: They go in the same backlog as features, ordered by the same logic, because they use the same team. I ask the Developers to state debt in business terms, such as slower changes to checkout, so we can compare it fairly, and we rely on the Definition of Done to avoid creating new debt. Critical production bugs are fixed immediately; other bugs are ordered like any item.

interview.q: How do you keep a backlog healthy?
interview.a: Short and honest: about two Sprints of ready items at the top, features for the next months, epics beyond. I archive items untouched for months, merge duplicates, keep titles readable for stakeholders, and do a short health check every month. I would rather say no clearly than keep a request in the backlog that will never be built.
